 Trump approves death by firing squad for convicted US military base shooter, says Pentagon 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP) — United States (US) President Donald Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist who shot dead 13 people at a military base in 2009, the Pentagon said Monday.

Hasan’s execution for the attack at Fort Hood in Texas — which also wounded more than two dozen people — will be the first carried out by the US military since 1961.

Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth “has recommended — and President Donald J Trump has approved — death by US Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a post on X.

“The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgment day for Hasan has finally come,” Parnell wrote.

Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 for carrying out the Al-Qaeda inspired mass shooting at Fort Hood.

He chose to conduct his own defence during the trial but called no witnesses, gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges. Court-appointed defence attorneys expressed concern that he was seeking execution.

Hasan, US-born Muslim of Palestinian descent, opened fire on November 5, 2009, at a medical facility in the sprawling Fort Hood base, which served as a staging point for soldiers to deploy to combat zones.

Twelve of the dead and 30 of the wounded were soldiers. Hasan was shot by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack and is partially paralysed.

The court that convicted Hasan was told that he was opposed to the US military’s occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he had spoken online with an alleged Al-Qaeda figure, radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, an American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.

news.title: Elon Musk’s heartbroken baby mama Shivon Zilis reveals billionaire has ended their relationship with no warning…’I’ve loved him more than life itself’
news.text:
By DANA KENNEDY, SENIOR INVESTIGATIVE REPORTER and EMILY CRANE 17:02 02 Oct 2026, updated 09:11 03 Oct 2026

Elon Musk’s longtime love and baby mama Shivon Zilis has revealed the billionaire abruptly ended their relationship ‘with no warning’ – with the mom-of-four declaring ‘it’s hard to go from in love to let go in a week.’

‘Hurting’ Zilis, an executive at Musk’s brain implant startup Neuralink, poured her heart out in a lengthy X post on Friday – just hours after eagle-eyed social media users noticed the billionaire had stopped following her on the platform he owns.

‘I’ve loved him more than life itself and he’s taught me 100 lifetimes of knowledge and made my cup overflow with life meaning, so there is a lot of loss, but luckily we created four beautiful little loves of my life,’ Zilis, 40, wrote on X.

‘I am so beyond grateful for our children and they make every single day the best day of my life! I do hope and pray he and I can be great friends and coparents.’

Zilis, who is believed to have first embarked on a secret tryst with the Space X founder back in 2016, went on to describe Musk as a ‘tortured soul.’

‘I feel happy that I got to show Elon how it feels to be deeply understood, nurtured, and peacefully loved with stability and gentleness,’ she wrote.

‘I loved being that counterbalancing place of safety, sense of calm, and love – and delighted in bringing a smile back to his face when he was down. I will miss him dearly.’

Zilis – the mother of four of Musk’s 14 kids – hinted, too, that she was blindsided by the breakup – sharing a screenshot of loved-up text messages the pair had exchanged just last week.

‘It was really wonderful to see you for breakfast. Love you very much,’ Zilis texted Musk.

‘Love you too. I didn’t realize that this Xi dinner included significant other (Beijing one did not) or I would have invited you,’ he responded on September 24, referencing the White House state dinner for the Chinese president. Zilis replied: ‘Aw, that means so much to me. Thank you.’

Musk, 55, hasn’t yet commented on the breakup.

Zilis ended her post by saying: ‘I’m hurting, but care deeply about E and will always be cheering for his happiness. God speed, Elon, the world is lucky to have you.’

The first apparent sign of trouble in the couple’s romance came back on September 28 when Zilis had posted a cryptic message on social media: ‘New day, new life.’

Then, earlier on Friday, Big Tech Alert, an account that tracks the online activity of technology figures, flagged that Musk had unfollowed her.

The Tesla founder only follows around 1,400 accounts.

News of the shock split comes just months after Zilis – who is one of four women Musk has children with – took the stand as a key witness in the Space X founder’s case against OpenAI earlier this year.

It was during her testimony that key details about their once-secret romance were laid bare.

Zilis, who was born in Ontario, Canada and studied at Yale University, had first met Musk through OpenAI – the artificial intelligence lab he co-founded in 2015.

She testified that their relationship began as ‘a one-off’ at a corporate off-site event – but later turned romantic around 2016.

Zilis told the jury that when she decided to have children as a single mom, Musk ‘offered to make a donation’ as a platonic sperm donor towards the end of 2020.

Their twins, Strider and Azure, were born by IVF in November 2021. News of their third child, Arcadia, surfaced in June 2024. And their son, Seldon Lycurgus, followed in February 2025.

Zilis testified that she lives in a house in Austin, Texas where Musk often stays when he visits their children.

Musk, for his part, called Zilis his ‘partner’ when it was his turn to testify.

The couple were spotted holding hands as they arrived at the wedding of White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino at President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate back in February.

Prior to becoming director of operations and special projects at Neuralink, Zilis had previously worked as a project director on Tesla’s Autopilot team from 2017 to 2019.

In the wake of their split, it wasn’t immediately clear whether Zilis would keep her roles at Neuralink and Musk’s other companies.

The Daily Mail has reached out to Zilis and Musk.

news.title: World News | US Picks Laser, Microwave Weapons Against Drones
news.text:
Washington, DC [US], October 6 (ANI): The United States Department of War has chosen four high-energy laser and high-powered microwave weapon systems for operational evaluation, marking a significant step as Washington seeks to broaden its capabilities in countering growing unmanned aerial vehicle threats targeting the homeland.

These platforms will undergo assessment through a directed-energy pilot initiative managed by Joint Interagency Task Force 401, the military command tasked with coordinating strategies against small unmanned aircraft systems.

Also Read | Israel Was Prepared To Shoot Down Flydubai Flight FZ1073 With 150 People Aboard After Cockpit Attack: Report.

The chosen platforms comprise AeroVironment's Palletised High-Energy Laser, Epirus' Leonidas High-Powered Microwave system, Kord's Firefly High-Energy Laser, alongside Boeing's Compact Laser Weapon System.

The Pentagon disclosed these selections on Monday, characterising the initiative as the subsequent phase in broader undertakings to scale up field utilisation of directed-energy technologies.

Also Read | Donald Trump Claims Iran Behind Flydubai Attack.

Highlighting the strategic value of these capabilities, US Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, who directs JIATF 401, stated, “High-energy lasers and high-powered microwave systems are tools that can be effectively used in a layered drone defence."

Brig. Gen. Ross further noted, “This pilot program will test these capabilities in an operational environment so we can understand how best to integrate and sustain them to defend the homeland."

Directed-energy armaments present a viable alternative to traditional projectiles and missiles when neutralising aerial drones.

Whilst high-energy lasers focus intense thermal energy onto specific targets, high-powered microwave platforms project electromagnetic pulses to disrupt internal electronic circuitry, furnishing an additional tier of protection against unmanned aircraft.

The Department of War noted that the Federal Aviation Administration, working alongside the task force, previously executed a safety risk evaluation during a live-fire laser demonstration hosted at the White Sands Missile Range situated in New Mexico.

Following those trials, aviation authorities concluded that the technology presented negligible hazards to the National Airspace System, subsequently establishing procedural parameters for ongoing cooperation, according to the department.

Ensuring the safety of directed-energy assets remains paramount whenever such armaments undergo evaluation or potential deployment within domestic American airspace.

Emphasising the tactical limitations of individual technologies, Brig. Gen. Ross stated, “There is no silver bullet, or one size fits all solution to countering the threat of drones."

He added, “Directed energy gives commanders another option within a layered defence, complementing existing counter-UAS capabilities with a scalable, safe, and effective way to respond to drone threats."

The task force director explained that field testing will supply critical data required to establish how these armaments might be deployed for domestic defence objectives.

Although these four armaments represent the initial cohort chosen for the pilot project, the Pentagon indicated it will persist in appraising supplementary directed-energy innovations.

An independent directed-energy competitive demonstration is slated for December at the Dugway Proving Ground located in Utah. That upcoming evaluation will appraise alternative high-energy laser and microwave assets to pinpoint potential candidates for prospective operational deployment.

Counter-drone defence mechanisms have evolved into a primary financial commitment for the US armed forces, as low-cost unmanned vehicles repeatedly illustrate their capacity to menace military facilities, active personnel, and vital infrastructure. (ANI)

news.title: Trump Allowed the Destruction of Two Major US Cities in a War with Iran
news.text:
Donald Trump suggested the destruction of Los Angeles and San Diego in the context of a war with Iran. The American leader made this statement at a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, where he was speaking in support of Republican Senator Pete Ricketts, Mediaite reports.

Speaking about the rise in gasoline prices due to the war with Iran, the president called them a small price for the security of the USA and the world.

"And once again, remember: with the war, it's all artificial," he told rally-goers. "Prices are a little high. That's a small price to pay to keep the world safe and our country safe.

 They can destroy a city. Let them destroy Los Angeles. Let them destroy San Diego. This is a very small price, and it will all be over very quickly. In fact, it's almost over already.

Or maybe they'll continue a little longer. You know, they always say, "They have a high pain threshold." They need it, believe me. But it will all be over very quickly. And it will end one way or another. And your gas, gasoline, and everything else..."

When Trump said, "Let them destroy Los Angeles or San Diego," the crowd applauded and cheered his words.

It is unclear whether the president was envisioning a scenario where these two cities had already been destroyed, or proposing that their destruction be permitted.

"Don't forget, we took on a country called Venezuela," he continued. "They never talk about Venezuela. We're getting hundreds of millions of barrels of oil. We're filling the country with oil in volumes no one has ever seen."

A similar referendum is scheduled to take place in two weeks in another province — Alberta.

news.title: Who Is Nidal Hasan? Trump Green-Lights Firing Squad for Fort Hood Shooter
news.text: President Donald Trump on Monday approved the execution of former Army Major Nidal Malik Hasan, the military psychiatrist convicted of carrying out the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, one of the deadliest attacks ever on a U.S. military installation. The Pentagon said Hasan is to be executed by firing squad, a rare method that would make him the first military prisoner executed since 1961. Trump's approval moves the case into the next stage of the military death penalty process, though further litigation in civilian federal court could still delay the execution. The decision comes days after a failed attempt to execute Tennessee death-row inmate Christa Pike by lethal injection renewed scrutiny of execution procedures and prompted Governor Bill Lee to halt the state's remaining executions this year. The decision has also renewed attention on Hasan, whose November 5, 2009, attack left 13 people dead and more than 30 others wounded at what is now Fort Cavazos, then known as Fort Hood. Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, was sentenced to death in 2013 after admitting he carried out the attack. Prosecutors described the shooting as an act of terrorism inspired by extremist Islamist beliefs. Army Psychiatrist Turned Convicted Mass Killer Born and raised in Virginia to parents who emigrated from a Palestinian town near Jerusalem, Hasan joined the Army after high school and attended medical school through a military scholarship program. He later trained as a psychiatrist and worked at Walter Reed Army Medical Center, where he treated service members returning from combat deployments in Iraq and Afghanistan. Those who knew Hasan before the attack often described him as quiet, religious and intensely private. Former colleagues and relatives later described him as increasingly troubled by the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and unhappy about the possibility of a deployment overseas. His cousin, Nader Hasan, described a deployment as "probably his worst nightmare." Military supervisors reportedly documented professional difficulties before the shooting. The Associated Press reported at the time that Hasan received a poor performance evaluation while working at Walter Reed and required additional counseling and supervision. Investigators also examined online postings attributed to someone using Hasan's name that appeared to justify violence committed in defense of Muslims, though officials never conclusively established that he wrote the messages. The Fort Hood Attack On November 5, 2009, Hasan entered a processing center at Fort Hood where soldiers were preparing for deployment. Witnesses said he shouted "Allahu Akbar," Arabic for "God is great," before opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun. Thirteen people were killed and more than 30 others wounded in the attack, making it one of the deadliest shootings ever carried out on a U.S. military base. Hasan was shot by civilian police officers responding to the scene but survived. He was left partially paralyzed and has spent years incarcerated at the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. During his court-martial, Hasan largely declined to challenge the government's case. Instead, he openly acknowledged being the shooter and told jurors that evidence would show he carried out the attack. He described himself as a soldier who had "switched sides" and argued that his actions were intended to prevent U.S. troops from deploying to Muslim countries. A military jury convicted him of 13 counts of premeditated murder and dozens of counts of attempted murder before sentencing him to death in 2013. Firing Squad Decision Follows Failed Tennessee Execution Trump approved Hasan's execution by firing squad days after Tennessee's failed attempt to execute Pike by lethal injection renewed scrutiny of execution procedures. Pike remained alive after prison officials administered two doses of pentobarbital on September 30. She was transported to a hospital, where she is on a ventilator, according to her attorney, and Lee subsequently halted the state's remaining executions for 2026 and ordered a comprehensive third-party review. The Pentagon has not said the Tennessee case influenced the decision to execute Hasan by firing squad. Military executions are exceptionally rare. Only four inmates, including Hasan, remain on military death row at Fort Leavenworth. The last person executed by the U.S. military was Army Private John Bennett, who was hanged in 1961 after being convicted of raping and attempting to murder an 11-year-old girl. If Hasan's execution proceeds, it would be the first carried out by the U.S. military in more than six decades and the first Army firing-squad execution since Private Eddie Slovik was executed for desertion during World War II in 1945. What Happens Next? Hasan's conviction and death sentence have already survived the military appellate process. The Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces affirmed his conviction and sentence in March 2024, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal in March 2025. Trump's approval triggers the next procedural stage. The secretary of the Army will determine the time and place of the execution. Army policy calls for an execution to occur no sooner than 60 days and no later than 150 days after presidential approval, although additional litigation could alter that timetable. Hasan may still seek habeas corpus review in civilian federal court, a process that legal experts say could delay the execution for years. A previous military execution approved by a president never took place. President George W. Bush approved the execution of Army Specialist Ronald Gray in 2008, but court action halted the execution, and Gray remains on military death row. The decision is also consistent with Trump's support for capital punishment. The federal government carried out 13 executions between 2020 and early 2021 after Trump resumed federal executions following a lengthy hiatus. For the families of those killed at Fort Hood, Monday's announcement marks the most significant development in the case in years. But despite Trump's approval, Hasan's execution is not necessarily imminent, and the case could remain tied up in court well before a final execution date is set. Why is Zimbabwe suddenly back on Donald Trump’s radar? Here’s what is driving renewed US interest in Zimbabwe.

0 President Trump to send delegation to Zimbabwe. Image via X@FonsiLoaiza Zimbabwe is suddenly attracting renewed attention from Washington, with United States President Donald Trump expected to send a delegation to Harare for talks with President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

The potential visit follows a meeting between Mnangagwa and Republican Congressman Marlin Stutzman on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month.

According to Zimbabwean officials, Stutzman subsequently briefed Trump on his discussions with Mnangagwa, leading to the proposal for a congressional and business delegation to Zimbabwe.

But why is Zimbabwe back on the US radar?

One major factor is Zimbabwe’s mineral wealth.

The country is seeking to position itself as an important player in the global energy transition, particularly through the extraction and local processing of minerals required for modern industries.

Zimbabwe has significant deposits of lithium, platinum-group metals, nickel and chrome, among other minerals.

Zimbabwe has increasingly pushed for investment in local processing rather than simply exporting raw minerals, creating opportunities for foreign companies seeking access to strategic mineral supplies.

This could make Zimbabwe an increasingly important economic partner as countries compete for secure critical-mineral supply chains.

Trade is another reason for the renewed engagement.

The United States has included Zimbabwe in its fiscal 2027 tariff-rate quota for raw cane sugar, giving the country an allocation of 813 metric tonnes.

The quota allows qualifying sugar imports to enter the US at a lower tariff rate than quantities outside the quota.

The move places Zimbabwe alongside other African countries, including South Africa, Mozambique and Malawi, which also have allocations under the US sugar programme.

While the allocation is relatively small, it provides Zimbabwean producers with an opportunity to access the American market.

The potential thaw also comes against the background of Zimbabwe’s more than two decades of difficult relations with Washington.

The Zimbabwe Democracy and Economic Recovery Act (ZDERA), passed in 2001, has long been a major point of contention between the two countries.

A US bill proposing the repeal of ZDERA has also been introduced, although any change to the legislation would require the US legislative process to run its course.

For Zimbabwe, improved relations with Washington could therefore have implications far beyond diplomacy.

Zimbabwe and US officials have indicated that high-level visits, trade and investment are among the issues being discussed.

If the proposed delegation travels to Harare, attention will turn to whether the engagement produces concrete deals on minerals, agriculture, investment and trade.

For now, the developments suggest that Washington and Harare are exploring a more commercially focused relationship after years of strained ties.

news.title: Secessionist Parti Quebecois wins Quebec election in Canada  - Haiti Gazette – Daily Haiti News
news.text:
The secessionist Parti Quebecois has won the most seats in Quebec’s election and will form the next government in the predominantly French-speaking Canadian province, according to media reports.

The result on Monday revives the question of whether the province should leave Canada, testing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s message of national unity.

Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, the party’s leader, is set to become premier.

During the campaign, he promised a third referendum on leaving Canada during his first term, although he said he would wait until US President Donald Trump leaves office in January 2029.

It was not yet clear whether the party had reached the 64 seats needed for a majority in the 127-seat National Assembly.

If it falls short, it would lead a minority government and need support from opposition lawmakers to pass major legislation and survive confidence votes.

The Parti Quebecois, or PQ, last governed the province from 2012 to 2014.

Monday’s victory marks a sharp recovery for the PQ, which won just three seats in the 2022 provincial election.

Its return also ends eight years in power for the Coalition Avenir Quebec, or CAQ, a centre-right Quebec nationalist party that does not support independence.

Daniel Beland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal, told The Associated Press news agency that the victory reflects Quebec’s multiparty system, where support is divided among several parties, rather than a surge in secessionist sentiment.

Support for independence remains at about 30 percent, low by historical standards, he said.

Still, Beland said a secessionist government in Quebec represents a new national-unity challenge for Carney, particularly with another independence-related vote approaching in Alberta.

“Seeing that a pro-independence party won in Quebec barely two weeks before an independence-related referendum takes place in Alberta might suggest to the Trump administration that national unity remains a major issue in Canada despite the popularity of Mark Carney,” Beland said.

Quebec held two previous referendums on independence, in 1980 and 1995, and voters rejected secession both times.

The second vote was decided by a narrow margin, but there has been no further referendum in the three decades since.

news.title: Secessionist Parti Quebecois wins Quebec election in Canada  - Guyana Inquirer – Daily Guyana News
news.text:
The secessionist Parti Quebecois has won the most seats in Quebec’s election and will form the next government in the predominantly French-speaking Canadian province, according to media reports.

The result on Monday revives the question of whether the province should leave Canada, testing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s message of national unity.

Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, the party’s leader, is set to become premier.

During the campaign, he promised a third referendum on leaving Canada during his first term, although he said he would wait until US President Donald Trump leaves office in January 2029.

It was not yet clear whether the party had reached the 64 seats needed for a majority in the 127-seat National Assembly.

If it falls short, it would lead a minority government and need support from opposition lawmakers to pass major legislation and survive confidence votes.

The Parti Quebecois, or PQ, last governed the province from 2012 to 2014.

Monday’s victory marks a sharp recovery for the PQ, which won just three seats in the 2022 provincial election.

Its return also ends eight years in power for the Coalition Avenir Quebec, or CAQ, a centre-right Quebec nationalist party that does not support independence.

Daniel Beland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal, told The Associated Press news agency that the victory reflects Quebec’s multiparty system, where support is divided among several parties, rather than a surge in secessionist sentiment.

Support for independence remains at about 30 percent, low by historical standards, he said.

Still, Beland said a secessionist government in Quebec represents a new national-unity challenge for Carney, particularly with another independence-related vote approaching in Alberta.

“Seeing that a pro-independence party won in Quebec barely two weeks before an independence-related referendum takes place in Alberta might suggest to the Trump administration that national unity remains a major issue in Canada despite the popularity of Mark Carney,” Beland said.

Quebec held two previous referendums on independence, in 1980 and 1995, and voters rejected secession both times.

The second vote was decided by a narrow margin, but there has been no further referendum in the three decades since.

news.title: Trump says his super PAC will now pay for controversial taxpayer-funded promo ads
news.text:
President Donald Trump said Monday night that he will no longer use taxpayer funds to pay for a multimillion-dollar pro-Trump ad blitz ahead of the midterm elections, saying his super PAC will now pay for them. 

While he dismissed criticism of the ads as "a rather standard thing to do," he said he had decided to run them on his own dime rather than that of the U.S. government in a post on his social media platform.

"I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc," Trump wrote, referring to his super PAC.

The move comes after the U.S. government bankrolled a series of ads that aired nationally and heavily featured the president. One of the ads was a direct copy of a spot Trump's campaign ran in 2024.

A White House official confirmed to ABC News Monday night that MAGA Inc. will pay for ads moving forward but defended them as something previous administrations have used.

"Presidential Public service announcements are nothing new. Administrations of both parties have used public service announcements to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction," the official said.

Earlier Monday, Vice President JD Vance defended using taxpayer money to run the ads, claiming they are "public service announcements."

"They're not partisan. They're not -- you know, it's not like we're advocating for a particular candidate. We're trying to tell a story, I think, about how great the United States of America is," Vance said.

Trump defended the ads last week at an event in the Oval Office, saying they were "for the spirit of our country" and not a political endorsement for Republican candidates on the ballot this November or for his administration's policies.

"You have to understand; I'm not promoting a candidate. I'm not promoting myself because I'm not running for office. I'm promoting the country," Trump said. 

"Now, if somebody said that that's wrong, I'll gladly pay the money. But these are ads for the country," he said.

Trump has implored Republican voters to "pretend" that he is on the ballot in the November midterm elections to boost voter turnout for GOP congressional candidates.

The federal government has spent at least $2.5 million to air the TV ads, according to an estimate from AdImpact, an advertising agency that analyzes ad spending across television.

A total of $20 million from the Department of Homeland Security's budget had been allocated for the effort.

Ethics watchdogs and several Congressional Democrats -- as well as some Republicans -- have said the ads are inappropriate. Some critics have said the ads could violate federal propaganda law.

Four ads have been aired over the last two weeks. One features Trump in monochrome, slowly walking down a hallway, describing "the final battle" against "the deep state," "the globalists," and "the sick political class that hates our country."

Another ad includes a montage of clips and images of Trump at events and rallies featuring onscreen text about the "largest tax cuts in history."

The latest ad, released last week, focuses on the U.S. war with Iran, now in its eighth month. Audio of Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plays in the background as U.S. military footage, including unclassified strikes, is displayed.

The video in the ad appears to be the same as one played during the Republican midterm convention last month. And it played last Wednesday before Hegseth addressed 600 service members in his State of the Force speech at the Marine Corps base at Quantico, Virginia.
news.summary: Trump says that he will no longer use taxpayer funds to pay for a pro-Trump ad blitz ahead of the midterm elections, saying his super PAC will now pay for them.

news.title: Trump Calls Russia’s Suspected Plague Case a ‘Big Problem’ as Nearly 200 Reportedly Monitored
news.text:
US President Donald Trump called Russia’s suspected pneumonic plague case a “big problem” on Monday as unofficial reports indicated that nearly 200 people were under observation following the death of a researcher at a Siberian infectious-disease laboratory.

“I hate to see them having it,” Trump said. “It’s a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter, like an army.”

Asked about the risk of the disease spreading internationally through travel, Trump appeared to play down the immediate threat, saying there was little travel headed toward the affected area.

The White House has said it is monitoring the situation in Russia and beyond after the researcher died days after being diagnosed with pneumonia of “unknown origin,” according to a Russian health agency.

Speaking on CNN, Dr. Ashish Jha, a former White House COVID-19 response coordinator and infectious-disease expert, said the circumstances surrounding the death raised “a lot of red flags.”

Jha pointed to reports that nearly 200 people were under observation, that several hospitals had been locked down and that Russia’s FSB security service had become involved in the response.

“That is not what you would expect from a simple lab accident,” Jha told CNN.

He also raised concerns about the history of the laboratory itself, saying it is officially described as a civilian facility but has longstanding links to military biological research.

Jha further said Russia has been expanding its biological-weapons capabilities, arguing that the combination of the laboratory’s history, the scale of the quarantine measures and the limited information released by Russian authorities warranted closer scrutiny.

“Take those two facts, take the facts that you just mentioned, it is hard not to be concerned that there is something more going on,” Jha said.

He stressed, however, that there was no confirmed evidence the researcher had been exposed to a weaponized pathogen.

Russian opposition figure and former world chess champion Garry Kasparov, also speaking to CNN, argued that the Kremlin’s lack of transparency made official Russian accounts difficult to trust.

Kasparov said Russia was operating on a war footing and suggested the laboratory could have been involved in military biological research, though he offered no direct evidence that the researcher’s death was connected to a weapons program.

“Whatever they said, they lied,” Kasparov said of Russian authorities, arguing that official statements from Moscow should be treated with deep skepticism.

Dr. Jonathan Reiner, a CNN medical analyst, urged caution, saying there was still no independent confirmation that the researcher had died from plague or clarity about how she became infected.

“It’s hard to know until we have more information,” Reiner said, adding that early reports during disease outbreaks are often “wrong, or incomplete, or misleading.”

He cautioned against jumping to either extreme – assuming the incident marked the beginning of another pandemic or dismissing it as nothing to worry about.

Reiner also stressed that pneumonic plague is very different from COVID-19. The disease has been known for centuries and can be treated effectively with antibiotics when detected early.

CNN separately reported that roughly 200 people were under quarantine or medical observation, while hospitals in the area had imposed restrictions and Russian officials said the woman died from severe pneumonia of unknown origin.

Russian authorities quarantined people connected to the Siberian research facility after the researcher’s death, while health officials stopped short of confirming pneumonic plague as the cause.

Officials in the Irkutsk region said the woman had died from severe pneumonia of “unknown origin,” even as restrictions around the facility expanded and questions grew over the circumstances of her illness. Russian authorities also publicly denied reports that pneumonic plague had been confirmed.
news.summary: Trump publicly addressed Russia’s suspected pneumonic plague case for the first time, calling it a “big problem.” CNN experts cited the scale of monitoring, FSB involvement and the lab’s history of military biological research as reasons for concern, while stressing that no weaponized pathogen has been confirmed.

WASHINGTON, October 6. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, an American of Palestinian descent and a military psychiatrist who killed 13 people and wounded 32 others in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, Assistant to the Secretary of War for Public Affairs Sean Parnell said.

news.title: Trump eases restrictions on dyed diesel, orders excise-tax deferral
news.text:
Oct. 5 (UPI) -- President Donald Trump on Monday night signed an executive order temporarily easing restrictions on red-dyed "off-road" diesel, directing that it be made available for highway use and that its federal excise tax be deferred as he attempts to lower surging diesel prices.

The order directs the secretaries of the Treasury, Transportation and Agriculture to expand access to dyed diesel, which is regular diesel fuel dyed red to indicate it is exempt from federal highway fuel taxes and is generally restricted to off-road uses, such as farming, construction equipment and heating, from Monday through Dec. 31.

It also directs the Treasury to defer the federal excise tax that would normally become due when dyed diesel is used in highway vehicles and to explore ways to eliminate the obligation to pay the tax when due. The repayment date was not stated.

A White House fact sheet claims that American truckers will save more than $100 per tank.

Trump announced the executive order during a rally for Republican Sen. Peter Ricketts in Grand Island, Neb., calling it "historic." Natalie Harp, Trump's special executive assistant, brought him the document, which he then signed at the lectern as the crowd cheered.

Trump signed the executive order as diesel prices have soared in the United States amid a global supply shortage worsened by the U.S. war against Iran and the years-long war between Ukraine and Russia.

According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, on-highway diesel fuel costs $6.38 as of late September, up $2.62 from a year earlier.

Trump has blamed the cost of diesel on Ukraine, which has for years attacked Russian refineries to squeeze the Kremlin's energy revenue that funds the war. Last month, Trump said he told President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine to stop attacking Russia's diesel-fuel-producing refineries, stating "he's causing a shortage of diesel fuel."

On his Truth Social account earlier Monday, Trump claimed that the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy route that has been restricted by Iran, was "no longer" driving high gas prices, instead blaming Ukraine for attacking Russia's refineries and claiming Democratic-led states were closing theirs. 

Several Republicans were quick to celebrate Trump's executive order online. Rep. Jason Smith of Missouri called it "a much-needed step to lessen the burden that increased fuel prices have had on farmers, ranchers and the entire agricultural community," and Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said it was "a HUGE WIN."
news.summary: President Donald Trump on Monday night signed an executive order temporarily easing restrictions on red-dyed "off-road" diesel.

news.title: US bill seeks steep H-1B fraud penalties
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 6 (IANS) A Republican lawmaker has introduced legislation that would raise penalties for serious H-1B visa violations to as much as $250,000, extend some employer sponsorship bans to at least 10 years and sharply increase fines for immigration document fraud. Rep. Beth Van Duyne of Texas announced the H-1B Visa Fraud Crackdown Act on Monday, saying existing penalties were too small to deter employers from abusing the programme. The legislation, H.R. 10643, is co-sponsored by Republican Reps. Brian Babin, Pat Fallon, Brandon Gill, Keith Self and Pete Sessions, all of Texas. "When a business can lie to the government and push American workers aside for cheaper labor, and the worst it faces is a $5,000 fine, many view that as the cost of doing business," Van Duyne said. "The H-1B Visa Fraud Crackdown Act changes the penalties. American jobs should go to American workers, and fraudsters should face real accountability for their actions." The bill would raise the maximum civil penalty for covered willful H-1B violations from $5,000 to $100,000. Van Duyne's office said those violations could include lying about the job being performed or underpaying an H-1B worker. For violations involving the willful displacement of US workers, the maximum civil penalty would increase from $35,000 to $250,000. The statutory changes are contained in the two-page legislation introduced in the House. Employers found responsible for serious willful violations would also face longer periods during which they could not sponsor H-1B workers. The minimum sponsorship ban would increase from two years to five years for serious willful violations. For violations that also involve displacement of US workers, the minimum ban would increase from three years to 10 years. The legislation would separately impose substantially higher penalties for immigration document fraud. For covered violations, penalties currently ranging from $250 to $2,000 would increase to between $1,000 and $10,000 per document. For violations following a previous order, fines would rise from the current $2,000-$5,000 range to between $20,000 and $50,000 per document. Van Duyne linked the legislation to allegations of H-1B fraud in North Texas. Her office said Homeland Security Secretary Mullin had confirmed that, as of June, nearly 60 per cent of H-1B employer fraud investigations nationwide were concentrated in the North Texas region. Van Duyne's office also said Labor Department Inspector General D'Esposito visited North Texas in August and found nearly 500 instances of likely H-1B visa fraud in a single building. It said no one answered the door at addresses he visited where an H-1B application had been approved. Those figures were presented by Van Duyne's office and were not contained in the text of the legislation. "I'm thankful for the Administration's quick response," Van Duyne said. "American workers should not lose opportunities because an employer is willing to break the law to get cheaper labor. If a business decides it makes more economic sense to break the law and kick American workers to the curb, they should feel major pain for undercutting our economy and our hardworking employees." The measure is proposed legislation and has not become law. It would have to clear the House and Senate and be signed by President Donald Trump before the higher penalties could take effect.

news.title: Democrats May Flip Longest-Held GOP Senate Seat for First Time in 107 Years
news.text: Democrats have their eyes on a potential upset in Kansas, where recent polls show the U.S. Senate race in a dead heat and the Cook Political Report rates the contest Lean Republican with roughly four weeks until Election Day. The position is held by Republican incumbent Senator Roger Marshall, a doctor, who is battling Democrat Adam Hamilton for the seat that has been held by the GOP since 1919, the longest ever for any party, High Plains Public Radio says. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Republicans now hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate. President Donald Trump carried Kansas by double digits over then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, underscoring the state’s Republican tilt. But Democrats have maintained a foothold in the state, with Laura Kelly in the governor’s mansion even as Republicans hold both U.S. Senate seats. Newsweek reached out to both Marshall and Hamilton's campaigns via email on Monday for comment. What To Know According to recent polling, Hamilton either leads by a very slim margin or the race is statistically tied. However, on prediction market site Kalshi Monday night, Marshall has 66 percent versus Hamilton's 34 percent. According to prediction market site Polymarket, Marshall has 68 percent compared to 33 percent for Hamilton. Cook says Hamilton is running an "increasingly strong race" and has been launching an attack ad against Marshall, an OB-GYN, over billing and collection practices at his office. Marshall has branded the ad targeting his practice a "lie." The forecaster also highlights that agriculture—and economic concerns impacting fertilizer and gas—are major factors in the Sunflower State and the rising prices make the race more competitive. Meanwhile, Marshall has branded Hamilton as a "radical Democrat," adding that "his sermons are identical to the Democratic Party platform." Democrats are hoping to capitalize on Trump's dropping approval ratings in state and national polls as the midterm elections loom. The president's overall approval and ranking on key policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have slipped as households across America are flagging affordability concerns. Robert Y. Shapiro, professor of political science at the School of International and Public Affairs at Columbia, told Newsweek on Monday when asked if Democrats realistically could flip the seat: "If this is a 'Wave' election it can flip. Or even otherwise since Hamilton is a very good moderate Democrat running against a very vulnerable opponent. This would be then a one off election unless this establishes a viable precedent for future Democratic candidates in Kansas. And possibly for Democrats elsewhere." What the Polls Show In a poll by The New York Times and Siena University last month, Marshall had 47 percent of the potential vote compared to 46 percent for Hamilton, and 7 percent of respondents said they did not know. The poll surveyed 605 likely voters from September 22 to September 30 and had a margin of error of 4.6 points. A Trafalgar Group poll shows Hamilton has 44.4 percent of the potential vote compared to 43.5 percent for Marshall, 2 percent for Libertarian Party candidate David C Graham and 10.1 percent are undecided. The poll surveyed 1,095 likely voters across the state from September 29 to October 1 and has a margin of error of 2.9 percent. A Wedgewood Polls survey last month showed Hamilton with 50 percent compared to Marshall's 48 percent and Graham's 2 percent. The poll surveyed 500 likely voters from September 22 to September 24 and had a 4.4 percent margin of error. Breakdown of Hamilton vs. Marshall Hamilton is pastor of the largest United Methodist Church in the country, the Church of the Resurrection. He founded the Kansas City-area church in 1990 at age 25, according to his campaign website. He won the Democratic Senate primary in August and is running on affordability; a theme Democrats across the country are emphasizing. His campaign is focused on bringing down energy, housing and healthcare costs as well as protecting Social Security, agriculture and ending “chaos and corruption” in Washington, D.C., his website says. Meanwhile, Marshall has been in the U.S. Senate since winning his 2020 election. He has been an OB-GYN in the state for 25 years, his campaign website highlights, and calls himself a fifth-generation "farm kid." Trump endorsed Marshall, labeling him a "strong advocate" for the people of Kansas. His campaign website touts bills from agriculture, border security and rural healthcare as a guide for voters to see what policies are important to the Republican. news.title: Trump targets tax-free diesel as Republicans approach midterms
news.text:
President Donald Trump on Monday took his Republican midterm rescue mission to Nebraska, where he signed an executive order to ease limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel, a decision he said would save “millions” for farmers and drive down the cost of all goods with just four weeks to go until the elections.

“Pete and Jim, this should absolutely ensure your election, I guarantee you that,” Trump said, addressing GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts, who is running against an independent candidate backed by national Democrats, and Gov. Jim Pillen, who is seeking a second term.

Diesel fuel prices have spiked in the aftermath of the Iran war, rattling voters and putting pressure on Republicans. Diesel fuel that is intended for off-road uses such as agriculture is exempt from federal and state excise taxes, and it is dyed for law enforcement purposes, the White House explained in a fact sheet. Temporarily removing the limits would reduce cost pressures on the businesses that rely on diesel.

“The typical trucker will save more than $100 every time they fill up,” Trump said, signing the executive order onstage before a crowd in Grand Island, Nebraska, in the solidly conservative south-central part of the state. He said the order will save farmers millions of dollars and drive down the cost of goods.

Read moreUS presses Europe to release diesel reserves 'immediately' as Trump threatens export ban

Patrick De Haan of GasBuddy, a platform that monitors national gasoline and diesel prices, noted last week, when news of the possible action began to surface, that such an order could save money for on-road users but not farmers, who already use red-dyed diesel.

"Taxes aren’t the problem, supply is," De Haan wrote on X.

Trump's trip is part of what the Republican president says is a 32-day blitz of rallies ahead of Nov. 3 that so far has taken him to ruby-red territory such as Oklahoma and Alabama. On Wednesday, he'll make his second stop in two weeks in Texas with a rally in San Antonio.

Ricketts, a former governor of the state, was appointed then later elected to fill Sen. Ben Sasse’s seat when he left to run the University of Florida in 2023. Now Ricketts is running for his first full six-year term against independent Dan Osborn – a race that initially was not expected to be competitive but is now being watched by the national parties.

Voters across the country are frustrated with Trump's handling of the economy, including persistently high costs for fuel and groceries. It's a major issue for rural voters who have backed the president and his party in recent elections.

Read moreEarly voting begins in US midterms that could see Republicans lose control of Congress

The administration’s plan to allow more imports of foreign beef has particularly roiled the agriculture-rich state of Nebraska. Trump wants to lower beef prices for consumers, but ranchers have rebelled against the import proposal, arguing it would undercut them.

“The plan to import low-quality foreign beef is not helping Nebraska ranchers,” Ricketts told the AP. “I would advise the White House to change that policy and look for longer-term things that will help us build the size of the herd and ultimately bring the price of beef down for consumers.”

In Grand Island, rally-goers said they they trusted Trump to solve the high cost of living.

“I feel like if we get our reserves built back up, get this situation in Iran taken care of, our gas prices will go down. The economy as far as groceries and stuff like that, it's going to go down too. It’ll stabilize. I have faith in him. More faith in him than I ever had in any other president," said Marlene Abel from Garfield, Kansas.

David Kuncl, who grew up on a farm, expressed confidence things would improve in the long run. But the Lincoln, Nebraska, resident insisted Trump wasn't to blame, pointing instead to what he believes is “a coup, a plot to try to hurt Trump" and the Republicans in the midterms.

Read moreUS hosts G20 energy talks in Texas as Iran war disrupts global fuel markets

“It’s hurting us. Gas prices. Diesel prices. Beef prices," he said. “I don’t know why they’re high. But it’s not that Trump’s got anything to do with that. He’ll do what he can. But of course he can’t wave a magic wand and make it go lower.”

In the House of Representatives, the Grand Island area is represented by Republican Rep. Adrian Smith, whose race is not expected to be close.

But Nebraska has a competitive House race farther east in Omaha, in the 2nd District – considered the “blue dot” of the state because the area’s electoral vote in presidential elections often goes to Democrats. The district is in the midst of a competitive race between Republican Brinker Harding and Democrat Denise Powell to fill retiring Rep. Don Bacon ’s open seat.

Monday's rally came as the Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC dedicated to electing Republicans to the House, cancelled $1.1 million in planned broadcast spending on behalf of the Republican candidate in the race, according to AdImpact, which tracks campaign media spending. It was a possible sign that GOP leaders feel the money could be put to better use elsewhere. The group did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

There are tentative plans for Trump to travel to other election battlegrounds, including Michigan, North Carolina, Georgia, Ohio, Kansas, Montana, Pennsylvania, Alaska, Nevada and Arizona before November’s Election Day. That’s according to a person familiar with the plans who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly and cautioned the plans could shift.
news.summary: President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order to ease limits on tax-free red-dyed diesel as fuel prices put pressure on Republican candidates. Trump said the move would save farmers millions of dollars and lower the cost of goods, though analysts said the change would not benefit farmers already using tax-exempt fuel.

news.title: US planning security strategy 10 years ahead
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 6 (IANS) President Donald Trump's national security team is conducting strategic planning that extends as far as five to 10 years into the future, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, describing a weekend meeting at Camp David as part of the administration's longer-term approach to global challenges. Rubio said the meeting brought national security officials together in a setting with fewer distractions and was not centred solely on immediate crises confronting the administration. "We constantly are meeting for long-term strategic planning and things of this nature," Rubio told reporters at Joint Base Andrews when asked about the Camp David meeting on Friday. "It's not unusual for us as a team to get together," he said. Rubio did not identify the specific issues discussed at Camp David or disclose who participated in the meeting. He said such sessions were part of the role played by the National Security Council in bringing together officials responsible for different areas of US national security policy. "That was just an opportunity to do it in a setting where there were less distractions, but we're constantly – that's just part of the role the National Security Council plays," Rubio said. The secretary offered an unusually broad description of the time horizon involved in the administration's strategic discussions. He said the NSC brings stakeholders together "to sort of do long-term planning – six months, nine months, but in many cases five or 10 years down the road." Rubio cautioned against characterising the Camp David session simply as routine, given the scope of the issues involved. "I wouldn't call it routine because the topics being discussed are global by nature, but they are long-term in thinking," he said. Rubio said the administration had held similar meetings previously and that the latest session differed principally because it took place at the presidential retreat. "We've had many meetings like that before. This one just happened to be in Camp David," he said. The secretary did not elaborate on what he meant by topics that were "global by nature." His comments came during a press interaction covering several immediate national security challenges, including Russia and Ukraine, fighting involving the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces, a suspected plague case in Russia and the security of US military installations in Britain. Rubio was speaking before departing on a trip that includes Iceland, Portugal and Greece, three NATO members. Asked about the European visit, Rubio described Iceland as a good friend of the United States and said the stop followed conversations with Icelandic leaders during the NATO summit earlier this year. He called Portugal a strong ally and described Greece as "a very important US ally," citing both the American military presence and strong economic ties. The National Security Council is the principal White House mechanism for coordinating national security and foreign policy across the US government. It brings together the president and senior officials responsible for diplomacy, defence, intelligence and other national security matters. Camp David, the presidential retreat in Maryland, has frequently been used by US presidents for high-level national security discussions, diplomatic meetings and strategic planning away from the day-to-day activity of the White House.

news.title: Oil prices slip as traders weigh strong Mideast exports against Gulf tensions
news.text:
Oil prices edged down on Tuesday as resilient Middle Eastern crude exports and a G7 ​emergency stockpile release eased supply concerns, though attacks by Yemen’s Houthis ‌on Saudi targets kept traders wary of risks to Gulf supplies.

Brent crude futures lost 4 cents to $100.28 a barrel by 0003 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude ​futures fell 11 cents, or 0.1%, to $89.33 a barrel.

“Oil is ​little changed after yesterday’s decline as traders continue to digest a ⁠modest easing in supply-side anxiety,” said KCM Trade chief analyst Tim ​Waterer.

“The pickup in Saudi export numbers and the G7 decision to release strategic ​reserves are helping keep a lid on prices for now, even while Brent remains anchored around the $100 level,” he said.

Crude exports from the Middle East exceeded pre-war levels ​on four days during the last week of September, shipping data showed ​on Monday, underscoring the resilience of regional oil flows despite attacks on ships passing ‌through ⁠the Strait of Hormuz.

news.title: Ex-Army major who killed 13 at Fort Hood set to be executed by firing squad
news.text: The former U.S. Army major who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009 will be executed by firing squad, officials said Monday. The Defense Department’s chief spokesperson, Sean Parnell, said death by firing squad for Nidal Hasan was recommended by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and approved by President Donald Trump. It would mark the first time the U.S. military has executed someone using the method since World War II. Hasan is a former Army major and psychiatrist who opened fire at Fort Hood on Nov. 5, 2009, killing 13 people and wounding 32 as he shouted “Allahu akbar,” Parnell said. He was convicted of premeditated murder in 2013 and sentenced to death. Prosecutors alleged he was motivated by unwillingness to be deployed to Afghanistan and by a sense of duty to jihad to kill as many American soldiers as possible, though a Joint Terrorism Task Force determined that he “was not involved in terrorist activities or terrorist planning,” and authorities said he acted alone. An Army prosecutor, Col. Steve Henricks, told the jury that Hasan had created a “personal kill zone” at Fort Hood the day of the attack. Hasan acted as his own lawyer during the trial and was convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder in 2013. Acting Army Secretary Adam R. Telle will set a time and place for the execution, Parnell said, adding, “Judgement day for Hasan has finally come.” Army Pvt. John Bennett was the last service member to be executed by the U.S. military — in 1961 by hanging. Pvt. Eddie Slovik was the last service member to be executed by firing squad in 1945, for desertion during World War II.
news.summary: Nidal Hasan’s execution by firing squad would mark the first time the U.S. military has put someone to death using the method since World War II.

news.title: Gavin Newsom, Jim Acosta and More Torch Trump After He Dares Iran to ‘Take Out’ Los Angeles or San Diego in Rally Speech
news.text:
Gavin Newsom, Jim Acosta and more ripped into Donald Trump Monday evening after the president appeared to dare Iran to “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego in a rally speech.

The controversy arose after Trump attempted to defend the ongoing military operation in Iran, telling rally attendees in Grand Island, Nebraska that it was a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.”

“They can take out a city,” Trump said. “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay. And it’s going to be over with very soon. It’s … almost over with – and they might keep going a little long. You know, they always say they have a big threshold for pain. They need it. Let me tell you. They need it. But it’s going to end very soon. And it will end one way or the other.”

It didn’t take long for Trump’s remarks to circulate on X, prompting a big reaction from California Governor Gavin Newsom.

“After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” Newsom wrote on X while sharing a clip of Trump’s comments. “He is deranged and dangerous.”

Veteran journalist Jim Acosta expressed a similar sentiment, writing on X, “The crowd starts to applaud as Trump fantasizes about LA and San Diego being wiped out by a nuclear attack. WTF. This is not normal.”

Additionally, Carrie Coon, the star of HBO’s “The Gilded Age,” pointedly wrote, “Can we take the keys away from Grandpa yet?”

While several of Trump’s supporters defended that the president was joking with the comment, several other X users made it clear they did not find the remark funny.

news.title: Trump approves firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon says
news.text:
The 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, for which Nidal Hasan was convicted, killed 13 US soldiers. Photograph: Tony Gutierrez/APView image in fullscreenThe 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, for which Nidal Hasan was convicted, killed 13 US soldiers. Photograph: Tony Gutierrez/APTrump approves firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon saysNidal Hasan sentenced to death by military jury in 2013 for carrying out deadly shooting attack at army base in Texas

Donald Trump has approved the execution by US army firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who was sentenced to death for killing 13 soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a social media post.

Hasan, who was an army psychiatrist, would become first US soldier to be executed by the US military in more than 60 years.

Parnell said in a post on X that defense secretary Pete Hegseth “has recommended – and President Donald J. Trump has approved – death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan”.

He added: “The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come.”

Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 for carrying out the mass shooting at the Fort Hood base.

He chose to conduct his own defense during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges. Court-appointed defense attorneys expressed concern that he was seeking execution.

Hasan, a US-born Muslim of Palestinian descent, opened fire on 5 November 2009 at a medical facility in the sprawling military base, which served as a staging point for soldiers to deploy to combat zones in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Twelve of the dead and 30 of the wounded were soldiers. Hasan was shot and partially paralyzed by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack.

The court that convicted Hasan was told that he was opposed to the US military’s occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that Hasan had spoken online with the radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, an al-Qaida propagandist and American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.

Although US mass shootings are disturbingly common, they are rare at military facilities.

In 2025, a soldier opened fire at a US military base in the state of Georgia, wounding five fellow troops before he was tackled and apprehended.

In 2019, a US sailor fatally shot two people and wounded a third at a base in Hawaii, while a Saudi military student shot dead three people at a military facility in Florida the same year.

A Kuwaiti-born US citizen attacked two military installations in Tennessee in 2015, killing four Marines and a sailor. The FBI concluded the violence was inspired by a “foreign terrorist group.”

Two years earlier, a man killed 12 people and wounded eight at the Washington Navy Yard in the US capital before being shot dead by officers.

news.title: Trump says taxpayers will no longer fund TV ads that praise him  - St. Lucia Chronicle – Daily St Lucia News
news.text:
United States President Donald Trump has said he will stop using taxpayer funds for television advertisements featuring him after widespread criticism of the campaign-style spots.

In a post on his social media site on Monday, Trump defended the advertisements, which cost at least $1.5m in federal funds and were aired ahead of the US November midterm elections.

Trump said he considered the advertisements to be “a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.”, but that they would no longer be funded by taxpayers but by either him or his MAGA PAC,

MAGA Inc. is Trump’s political war chest and had amassed more than $400m by the end of July.

The announcement came as ethics experts and lawmakers from both ⁠parties have criticised the three nationally broadcast advertisements and called for independent investigations.

The advertisements have run during football games as recently as Sunday and during other programming.

One features Trump declaring that “America will never be a communist country”, ⁠while a chorus repeats the words “love me”. Another combines ⁠images of Mount Rushmore with footage of Trump praising a “golden age of America”.

The advertisements end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for by the US government.

Democratic lawmakers said last month that the White House transferred $20m in Homeland Security Department funds to air ⁠the advertisements, including one that closely resembles a 2024 Trump ⁠campaign ad, and sought independent probes.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday called ‌for an independent investigation, calling it a “staggering misuse of public funding and breach of public trust” after the calls for a probe.

Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr, a ‌Republican ‌named to his position by Trump, last week said the advertisements were appropriate and rejected a request to investigate them.

news.text:

President Donald Trump on Monday criticized election officials in Arizona's Maricopa County after about 3,000 ballots were mistakenly mailed early to voters.The miscue, blamed on a vendor error, would have no effect on the voters who received the ballots, the county recorder's office said. The Maricopa County Recorder's Office, which is run by Republican Recorder Justin Heap, said Sunday that Runbeck Election Services told the office that it "mistakenly mailed 3,126 early ballots the previous day," six days before they were scheduled to be sent to voters for this year's midterm elections.Runbeck said the ballots were "processed separately from the primary mailing" because they did not qualify for automated mail processing from the U.S. Postal Service. Trump has frequently focused false claims of a stolen election in 2020 on the county.Heap and the Republican-controlled county of board of supervisors had been entangled for months in a prolonged legal battle over how to jointly run elections. news.title: Trump says US would help Russia amid reported fatal case of pneumonic plague
news.text:
President Donald Trump said the U.S. is willing to help Russia after the State Department announced it was monitoring a reportedly fatal case of "pneumonia of an unknown etiology" linked to a Russian plague research laboratory.

"Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we're always willing to help," Trump told reporters Monday.

Asked about how the U.S. is planning to mitigate the risk coming from Russia, Trump said that his administration is "looking at it very strongly."

Trump referred to the outbreak as the "pneumonia plague,” going on to describe pneumonia as a “rough disease,” adding “those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They're like an army.”

On Sunday, a spokesperson from the State Department said in a statement, "We are aware of ​reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia. We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners."

"Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly," the spokesperson added.

Where the case of plague has been detected

Health authorities in Russia's Irkutsk region launched anti-epidemic measures after an employee of a plague institute was diagnosed with "pneumonia of an unknown etiology," the country's sanitary watchdog agency, Rospotrebnadzor, confirmed on Sunday.

The lab involved is the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov, in southern Siberia, Russia. 

The statement comes after some Russian media and public figures reported a death potentially due to the plague and linked to a lab worker. Russian officials did not provide further details on the worker.

The Russian agency's statement said that "no accidents have been detected at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute while working with pathogenic microorganisms."

Their statement added that "the sanitary and epidemiological situation" in the Irkutsk Region, the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov, is "stable."

How Russian authorities are responding

Regional governor Igor Kobzev said in a statement on Friday that people who had contact with a resident who contracted a "particularly dangerous infection" were placed under medical observation.

Responding to the growing speculation, the governor on Monday said that "no microorganisms associated with the woman's professional activities were found in her biomaterials" and that no other lab workers have sought medical help in recent days. 

Officials said none of the identified contacts were showing symptoms so far and their laboratory tests were negative, according to Kobzev.

Before Rospotrebnadzor reported that the employee's illness was due to pneumonia with an unknown cause, Alexei Tsydenov, the head of Buryatia, a region neighboring Irkutsk Oblast, suggested that a woman may have died of the plague.

Citing Buryatia's health officials, Tsydenov wrote in a post on his Telegram channel on Friday that "the woman who died – possibly from the plague – in the Irkutsk Region had not visited Buryatia," assuring Buryatia residents that "there are no plague outbreaks in the republic."

Amid the investigation, some protective measures have been announced in the region. A mask mandate has been implemented at the Irkutsk Aluminum Plant in Shelekhov, according to the plant's director, Artem Fominykh. 

"Better safe than sorry," Fominykh wrote in a post on his Telegram channel on Saturday, asking the employees to "follow the precautions." He added that some conflicting information about the situation is circulating in Shelekhov, and urged the plant employees to seek medical attention immediately if they experience any symptoms.

US response

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said in a statement on Sunday that it is "monitoring the situation closely" with the State Department.

"The safety and security of U.S. citizens is our highest priority," the CDC said.

"Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly," a State Department spokesperson said in a statement.

"Plague is a known disease and is treatable with common antibiotics, especially when treatment starts early. Cases occur naturally in many parts of the world," the statement added.

What to know about plague and its transmission

Plague is a disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, according to the CDC.

Humans can contract the disease after being bitten by an infected rodent flea, coming into contact with contaminated fluid or tissue from an infected animal or by inhaling infected droplets in the air.

There are three types of plague: bubonic, pneumonic and septicemic. Symptoms often include fever, chills, and weakness.

Pneumonic is the most serious form and the only one that can potentially spread between people. It occurs when bacteria spread to the lungs of a patient with untreated bubonic or septicemic plague, or when a person inhales infectious droplets, according to the CDC. 

Bubonic plague is infamously responsible for the deaths of millions of people in Europe during the 1300s. While the disease still exists, modern medicine and public health efforts have made it less threatening.

Plague can be treated with a course of antibiotics. The earlier antibiotics are received, the higher are the chances of a full recovery.

The U.S. averages about seven cases of plague each year, mostly on the West Coast in states such as Arizona and New Mexico, according to the CDC. It's been more than a century since the U.S. has seen a documented case of person-to-person spread of plague, per the CDC.
news.summary: Health authorities in Russia’s Irkutsk region launched anti-epidemic measures after an employee of a plague institute died.

ReutersThe Parti Quebecois has regained power in Quebec's provincial election, ending eight years of Coalition Avenir Quebec rule.

Tornoto: The separatist Parti Quebecois won Quebec's provincial election Monday, returning to power a party that has promised another referendum on independence from Canada.The victory by Paul St-Pierre Plamondon's party ends eight years of rule by the Coalition Avenir Quebec and puts the question of Quebec's future in Canada back at the center of provincial politics.Also Read: Canada: Quebec to reopen major permanent residence pathway from July 2St-Pierre Plamondon has pledged to hold another referendum on independence, though he has said he would wait until U.S. President Donald Trump is no longer in office.The PQ won the most seats in Quebec's 127-member National Assembly, the provincial legislature, but it was not yet clear whether it would reach the 64 seats needed for a majority government.Live EventsIf the PQ falls short of 64 seats, it would lead a minority government and need support from opposition lawmakers to pass key legislation and survive confidence votes.Coalition Avenir Quebec leader Christine Frechette conceded defeat, saying voters had made their choice and that she took full responsibility for the "difficult result." The CAQ, which held 79 seats before the election, was at risk of losing every seat in the legislature.But the PQ's victory does not mean most Quebecers support leaving Canada.Daniel Beland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal, said the victory reflects Quebec's multiparty system, where support is divided among several parties, rather than a surge in separatist sentiment. Support for independence remains at about 30%, low by historical standards, he said.Beland said the result should not be viewed as a rejection of Prime Minister Mark Carney, who remains very popular in Quebec.Still, Beland said a separatist government in Quebec represents a new national-unity challenge for Carney, particularly with another independence-related vote approaching elsewhere in Canada.Also Read: Fraternité, Solidarité & the Tree: A small Quebec municipality, a big idea for the world's treesThe Quebec result comes two weeks before Albertans vote Oct. 19 on whether to hold a referendum on separation from Canada."Seeing that a pro-independence party won in Quebec barely two weeks before an independence-related referendum takes place in Alberta might suggest to the Trump administration that national unity remains a major issue in Canada despite the popularity of Mark Carney," Beland said.Quebec voters have twice rejected sovereignty, most recently by a razor-thin margin in a 1995 referendum.Quebec, which is about 80% French-speaking, already has significant autonomy. news.title: Border czar Tom Homan clashes with CBS interviewer over ICE migrant deaths, asks for Biden-era data
news.text:
Border czar Tom Homan accused a CBS journalist of asking a “loaded question” in a Friday interview about how ICE treats detained illegal migrants, asking him whether he gathered statistics about migrant deaths under the Biden administration.

CBS News’ immigration correspondent Camilo Montoya-Galvez asked Homan about deaths in ICE custody under the Trump administration, noting that this year could set a “new record high.”

“We looked at official ICE data, sir, and found that 57 people have died in the agency’s custody so far under this administration,” Montoya-Galvez said. “In fact, somebody was just reported to have died in ICE custody today by the agency. 2026 could set a new record high in the number of detainees dying. What is being done to prevent that? And I know one partial explanation is that more people are being detained and, so tragically, more people are dying. But that can’t be the only explanation, can it be?”

“How many people died during the Biden administration?” Homan immediately replied, followed by a long pause. “How many people died in custody during the Biden administration? Do you know?”

“A significant number,” Montoya-Galvez replied.

“Do you know?” Homan pressed further.

“But this is going to be the highest year in 2026,” Montoya-Galvez continued. “I’m just asking if the pace continues —”

“Do you know how many died during the Biden administration?” Homan pressed again.

“I don’t have the data here,” the CBS interviewer admitted.

“Of course you don’t,” Homan said. “Again, it’s another loaded question against the Trump administration.”

Homan said that ICE maintains the highest standards for detention centers.

“We have the highest detention standards in industry, higher than any state or federal institution. Our deaths in custody … are among the lowest of any state prison or Bureau of Prisons. Numbers are up because our population has doubled in custody. We got over 70 — I think the other day we had like 74,000 in custody,” he said. 

Homan went on to argue that the quality of ICE medical care is so high to the point detainees are helped with medical issues they didn’t even know they had.

“So we have more people in custody, and we’re dealing with people from third-world nations,” he said. “Some of the first doctors they see are our doctors. And matter of fact, no one ever talks about how many lives that ICE saves in detention when they found a serious medical issue that the alien didn’t even know about and we treat. When I was ICE director, I think we spent almost a billion dollars on medical care.”

He compared ICE detention to federal or state prisons.

“Again, it’s unfortunate, and it’s sad when anybody dies. I don’t want to see anybody die, but we do everything we can to give them the best medical care that we can provide. And again, highest detention standards,” Homan said. “I think if you look at deaths in custody compared to state prisons or federal penitentiaries, I think we’re one of the lowest. At least the last time I looked at the data — it was probably a couple years ago — we’re the lowest.”

Theo Wold, a former acting assistant attorney general and deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy during President Donald Trump’s first administration, criticized Montoya-Galvez’s questions in comments to Fox News Digital.

“This is what passes for journalism in modern America — a reporter comes prepared with gotcha questions but no backup data,” he said. “The purpose isn’t to inform the public (which ought to be the goal of journalism), it’s to manufacture ideological sound bites for the nightly news.” 

“No one wants in-custody deaths, but no administration can avoid them,” Wold added. “The Trump Administration has more than doubled Biden-era enforcement, which means more individuals detained and more in-custody deaths, most often through no fault of ICE or its enforcement officers.”
news.summary: Border czar presses interviewer on whether he had Biden-era custody death statistics before defending ICE standards
