news.title: Who Is Nidal Malik Hasan? Trump Approves Rare Army Firing Squad Execution of Fort Hood Shooter
news.text: US President Donald Trump on Monday approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hasan, the former Army officer convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell announced the decision on Monday, saying Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had recommended the execution and Trump had approved it. "Judgment day for Hasan has finally come," Parnell said in a post on X. Hasan was sentenced to death in 2013 after being convicted by a military court of carrying out the shooting at the Army base, now known as Fort Cavazos. The attack, which took place nearly 17 years ago, also left 32 people wounded. Witnesses said Hasan shouted "Allahu Akbar" as he opened fire on soldiers at a facility where troops were preparing to deploy to Iraq and Afghanistan. The 2009 attack was one of the deadliest incidents on a US military installation. Death Sentence and Appeals Hasan was arrested after being shot and wounded during an exchange of gunfire with police. He was court-martialled four years later and sentenced to death. His case was automatically subject to appeals under the military justice system. A military appeals court upheld the death sentence in 2025, while the US Supreme Court later declined to review the case after Hasan's lawyers raised procedural objections. The Pentagon said Trump’s approval clears the way for an Army execution, although further steps remain before it can take place. The Army secretary will determine the time and location of the execution, according to Parnell. Rare Military Execution If carried out, Hasan's execution would be the first US military execution authorised by a president since 1961. Pvt John Bennett was the last US service member to be executed, when he was hanged in April 1961 after being convicted of attempting to murder an 11-year-old girl in Austria. Former President George W Bush also approved a military execution in 2008, but a federal court intervened and prevented it from taking place. Military executions are governed by the Uniform Code of Military Justice and are separate from executions carried out under civilian state or federal law. Hasan's execution would therefore represent an exceptionally rare use of the military death penalty. The Fort Hood shooting prompted years of scrutiny over Hasan's motives, his conduct before the attack and the military's handling of warnings about him. The Army said after his sentencing that the case had caused profound suffering for the families of those killed and for survivors of the attack.
news.summary: If executed, Hasan's case would mark the first military execution approved by a president since 1961, highlighting a rare application of the military death penalty

news.title: Oil prices hover near $100 as Middle East supply holds up, Gulf risks persist
news.text: Oil prices remained close to $100 a barrel on Tuesday, with steady Middle Eastern oil exports helping to ease supply concerns. However, continued attacks in the region kept traders alert to the risk of disruptions to Gulf supplies.Brent crude was trading at $100.6 a barrel, up 24 cents or 0.24%, while WTI stood at $89.60, gaining 17 cents or 0.19%.The benchmarks have eased from around $103 a barrel after shipping data showed Middle Eastern crude exports had exceeded pre-war levels on four days in the final week of September. Why is Zimbabwe suddenly back on Donald Trump’s radar? Here’s what is driving renewed US interest in Zimbabwe.

0 President Trump to send delegation to Zimbabwe. Image via X@FonsiLoaiza Zimbabwe is suddenly attracting renewed attention from Washington, with United States President Donald Trump expected to send a delegation to Harare for talks with President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

The potential visit follows a meeting between Mnangagwa and Republican Congressman Marlin Stutzman on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month.

According to Zimbabwean officials, Stutzman subsequently briefed Trump on his discussions with Mnangagwa, leading to the proposal for a congressional and business delegation to Zimbabwe.

But why is Zimbabwe back on the US radar?

One major factor is Zimbabwe’s mineral wealth.

The country is seeking to position itself as an important player in the global energy transition, particularly through the extraction and local processing of minerals required for modern industries.

Zimbabwe has significant deposits of lithium, platinum-group metals, nickel and chrome, among other minerals.

Zimbabwe has increasingly pushed for investment in local processing rather than simply exporting raw minerals, creating opportunities for foreign companies seeking access to strategic mineral supplies.

This could make Zimbabwe an increasingly important economic partner as countries compete for secure critical-mineral supply chains.

Trade is another reason for the renewed engagement.

The United States has included Zimbabwe in its fiscal 2027 tariff-rate quota for raw cane sugar, giving the country an allocation of 813 metric tonnes.

The quota allows qualifying sugar imports to enter the US at a lower tariff rate than quantities outside the quota.

The move places Zimbabwe alongside other African countries, including South Africa, Mozambique and Malawi, which also have allocations under the US sugar programme.

While the allocation is relatively small, it provides Zimbabwean producers with an opportunity to access the American market.

The potential thaw also comes against the background of Zimbabwe’s more than two decades of difficult relations with Washington.

The Zimbabwe Democracy and Economic Recovery Act (ZDERA), passed in 2001, has long been a major point of contention between the two countries.

A US bill proposing the repeal of ZDERA has also been introduced, although any change to the legislation would require the US legislative process to run its course.

For Zimbabwe, improved relations with Washington could therefore have implications far beyond diplomacy.

Zimbabwe and US officials have indicated that high-level visits, trade and investment are among the issues being discussed.

If the proposed delegation travels to Harare, attention will turn to whether the engagement produces concrete deals on minerals, agriculture, investment and trade.

For now, the developments suggest that Washington and Harare are exploring a more commercially focused relationship after years of strained ties.

news.title: Chicago woman sues US government, says CBP agent fired at her from behind
news.text:
APMarimar Martinez filed a lawsuit against the federal government after being shot by a Customs and Border Protection agent.

Chicago: An American citizen shot by a Customs and Border Protection agent one year ago during a sweeping immigration crackdown in Chicago filed a lawsuit against the federal government on Monday, alleging the agent lied about the shooting and fired into her vehicle from behind.Federal prosecutors initially accused Marimar Martinez, then 30, of using her vehicle to strike and box in agent Charles Exum's SUV on Chicago's southwest side on Oct. 4, 2025, during "Operation Midway Blitz." Exum then exited his car and opened fire, leaving Martinez with seven gunshot wounds.In the month after the shooting, prosecutors filed to dismiss the charges in a dramatic reversal of the closely watched case in the nation's third-largest city.Agent fired into rear of car, attorneys sayHer lawyers said Monday that they commissioned an expert to analyze bullet trajectories and her injuries and determined Exum wasn't in the path of her car when he opened fire. They said he had walked several feet toward her car, contrary to statements he made to the FBI, and fired off five shots in less than a second, the last from the rear side of her vehicle."Charles Exum told the FBI agent on that day, within hours of the shooting, that Marimar was driving her car directly at him, that he shot her five times through the windshield, and that he ceased firing once he was no longer in the path of the vehicle. Those are three objective lies that you'll see here today," said one of her attorneys, Chris Parente.Live EventsParente said there were only three bullet holes in Martinez' windshield on the right passenger side, which indicated Martinez wasn't driving toward the agent. He said the fourth shot was fired through the front passenger side window, adding another bullet hole in the back of Martinez' car seat showed the agent fired the fifth shot from behind her."In what world can a U.S. law enforcement officer stand behind a car and fire his Glock service weapon through the rear passenger window at a young woman who's crouched over the steering wheel?" Parente said.CBP said in a statement to The Associated Press in response to the suit that Exum had been placed on administrative leave. Use-of-force incidents are "thoroughly investigated, reviewed, and presented" to an independent board, it added.Exum is not a defendant in the lawsuit against the federal government, which was filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act and does not allow for lawsuits against individual agents. It was not known where Exum could be reached.Body-worn camera footage from another agent in Exum's vehicle before the shooting captured the agents saying it was "time to get aggressive" and other profanity-laced comments by agents who were present encouraging violence, according to the complaint.Martinez taken from hospital with bullet holes 'leaking blood,' suit saysThe FBI arrested Martinez, taking her out of the hospital just hours after the shooting when she was "wheelchair bound and her bullet holes were leaking blood through her bandages," according to the lawsuit. A judge ordered her release two days after her arrest.Messages released by Martinez' attorneys in February showed that former head of Border Patrol Greg Bovino had praised Exum for his "excellent service in Chicago" after the shooting. Other messages they released showed agents in a group chat congratulating Exum and calling him a "legend."Martinez was one several people shot in their cars by federal agents during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown. An immigration agent shot a Venezuelan delivery driver in his car in Austin, Texas, last month, and another shot a Colombian driver in Biddeford, Maine, in July. The Trump administration has at times justified such shootings as self-defense against people allegedly weaponizing their vehicles.Martinez appeared with her attorneys at a news conference Monday, saying the various shootings spurred her to file suit."If I don't, then who else, you know? Look at what happened to Renee and all these victims," she said, referring to Renee Good, a woman shot dead in her vehicle by a federal agent in Minneapolis in January."What's happening is not normal. We shouldn't stay here and normalize what's happening," she said.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Trump 'personally' believes Iran responsible for attack by Omani co-pilot on FlyDubai flight
news.text: US President Donald Trump on Monday (local time) said he "personally" believes Iran was behind the attack carried out by an Omani co-pilot aboard a FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv."I do. I personally do," Trump said when asked whether he believed Iran was responsible for the attack on the flydubai flight. He was responding to media queries on the White House premises. The remarks came following the foiled mid-air hijacking and crash attempt aboard flydubai Flight FZ1073 on September 30, when Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami attacked Indian Captain Smit Machchhar inside the cockpit. The Omani co-pilot attacked Captain Machchhar with an axe in an attempt to bring down the aircraft. Despite suffering severe injuries, Captain Machchhar managed to unlatch the cockpit door, allowing passengers and off-duty crew members to enter and restrain the attacker.The confrontation triggered a steep descent, with the aircraft dropping approximately 16,000 feet within two minutes before a hijacking distress signal was transmitted.The aircraft was subsequently diverted and made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, with all 180 occupants disembarking without injury.Reports published on Sunday by The Times of Israel said al-Hammami had planned to direct the aircraft into Israel's Ben Gurion Airport. The reports, citing Hebrew media sources, said the Omani co-pilot was detained and undergoing interrogation in the United Arab Emirates..UAE presidential adviser calls Flydubai attack 'dangerous terrorist act', lauds Indian pilot.According to the reports, al-Hammami told investigators that his alleged plan was to operate the flight routinely after incapacitating Captain Machchhar, obtain the mandatory landing clearances and then crash the aircraft into an airport facility or a stationed aircraft.The attack was thwarted after Captain Machchhar, despite being severely injured, succeeded in opening the cockpit door.Captain Machchhar later described the impact of the initial assault, saying that after attempting to stop the attacker, his vision became severely blurred.The incident has drawn attention to the actions of Machchhar, who was praised by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as a "hero of Israel, India, and the world" during a video conference while the pilot was recovering.Following a direct phone call between Netanyahu and Machchhar, the Israeli government officially invited the Indian pilot and his family to attend Israel's Independence Day celebrations in May 2027.(With inputs from ANI).FlyDubai row: Trump claims Iran may be linked to co-pilot who tried to crash Israel-bound jet.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest
